title: Acts 19:21–41
context: Paul resolves in the Spirit to go through Macedonia and Achaia to Jerusalem and then to Rome. In Ephesus a silversmith named Demetrius, who makes shrines of Artemis, rouses the craftsmen by warning that Paul’s teaching threatens their trade and the goddess’s honor. The city fills with confusion, and the crowd rushes into the theater, shouting, “Great is Artemis of the Ephesians!” for two hours. The town clerk finally quiets them, points out that the Christians have not robbed temples or blasphemed the goddess, directs any complaint to the courts, and dismisses the assembly.

verses.text: Now after these things had ended, Paul determined in the Spirit, when he had passed through Macedonia and Achaia, to go to Jerusalem, saying, “After I have been there, I must also see Rome.”
verses.arminianNotes: Paul resolves in the Spirit to go to Jerusalem and then Rome. Arminian readers see Paul planning under the Spirit’s guidance.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers see the “must” of God’s plan taking Paul toward Rome.

verses.text: Having sent into Macedonia two of those who served him, Timothy and Erastus, he himself stayed in Asia for a while.
verses.arminianNotes: He sends Timothy and Erastus ahead to Macedonia. Arminian commentators see delegation in ministry.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed commentators see coordinated mission.

verses.text: About that time there arose no small disturbance concerning the Way.
verses.arminianNotes: A great disturbance arises concerning the Way. Arminian readers see the gospel provoking public reaction.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers see the world opposing Christ’s kingdom.

verses.text: For a certain man named Demetrius, a silversmith who made silver shrines of Artemis, brought no little business to the craftsmen,
verses.arminianNotes: Demetrius makes silver shrines of Artemis. Arminian expositors see a man whose income depends on idolatry.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed expositors see economic interests bound to false worship.

verses.text: whom he gathered together with the workmen of like occupation, and said, “Sirs, you know that by this business we have our wealth.
verses.arminianNotes: He gathers the craftsmen and reminds them their wealth comes from this trade. Arminian readers see motives exposed.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers see greed as a root of opposition.

verses.text: You see and hear that not at Ephesus alone, but almost throughout all Asia, this Paul has persuaded and turned away many people, saying that they are no gods that are made with hands.
verses.arminianNotes: Paul has persuaded many that gods made with hands are not gods. Arminian commentators see the message changing people’s choices.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed commentators see an unwilling testimony to the gospel’s power.

verses.text: Not only is there danger that this our trade come into disrepute, but also that the temple of the great goddess Artemis will be counted as nothing and her majesty destroyed, whom all Asia and the world worships.”
verses.arminianNotes: He fears their trade and Artemis’s temple will be discredited. Arminian readers see religion and money tangled together.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers see the idol’s glory threatened by the true God.

verses.text: When they heard this they were filled with anger, and cried out, saying, “Great is Artemis of the Ephesians!”
verses.arminianNotes: They are enraged and shout, “Great is Artemis of the Ephesians!” Arminian expositors see anger replacing reason.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed expositors see the futility of loud devotion to a false god.

verses.text: The whole city was filled with confusion, and they rushed with one accord into the theater, having seized Gaius and Aristarchus, men of Macedonia, Paul’s companions in travel.
verses.arminianNotes: The city is filled with confusion, and they seize Gaius and Aristarchus. Arminian readers see danger to Paul’s companions.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers see chaos under God’s control.

verses.text: When Paul wanted to enter in to the people, the disciples didn’t allow him.
verses.arminianNotes: Paul wants to go to the crowd, but the disciples stop him. Arminian commentators see wise friends protecting him.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed commentators see God using friends to preserve his servant.

verses.text: Certain also of the Asiarchs, being his friends, sent to him and begged him not to venture into the theater.
verses.arminianNotes: Some officials of Asia, his friends, urge him not to enter the theater. Arminian readers see Paul’s influence even with officials.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers see unexpected allies provided by God.

verses.text: Some therefore cried one thing, and some another, for the assembly was in confusion. Most of them didn’t know why they had come together.
verses.arminianNotes: The assembly is in confusion, and most do not know why they came. Arminian expositors see the irony of a mob without purpose.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed expositors see the emptiness of idolatrous zeal.

verses.text: They brought Alexander out of the multitude, the Jews putting him forward. Alexander beckoned with his hand, and would have made a defense to the people.
verses.arminianNotes: Alexander is pushed forward by the Jews to make a defense. Arminian readers see others trying to distance themselves.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers see confusion multiplying.

verses.text: But when they perceived that he was a Jew, all with one voice for a time of about two hours cried out, “Great is Artemis of the Ephesians!”
verses.arminianNotes: Recognizing him as a Jew, they shout for two hours. Arminian commentators see mob hostility.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed commentators see the persistence of idolatry.

verses.text: When the town clerk had quieted the multitude, he said, “You men of Ephesus, what man is there who doesn’t know that the city of the Ephesians is temple keeper of the great goddess Artemis, and of the image which fell down from Zeus?
verses.arminianNotes: The town clerk quiets them and affirms Ephesus as temple keeper of Artemis. Arminian readers see civic order restored.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers see God restraining violence through a civil official.

verses.text: Seeing then that these things can’t be denied, you ought to be quiet and to do nothing rash.
verses.arminianNotes: Since these things cannot be denied, they should do nothing rash. Arminian expositors see a calm voice of reason.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed expositors see providence turning the crisis.

verses.text: For you have brought these men here, who are neither robbers of temples nor blasphemers of your goddess.
verses.arminianNotes: The men are neither temple robbers nor blasphemers of the goddess. Arminian readers see the believers’ conduct vindicated.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers see the gospel advancing without insulting people.

verses.text: If therefore Demetrius and the craftsmen who are with him have a matter against anyone, the courts are open and there are proconsuls. Let them press charges against one another.
verses.arminianNotes: If Demetrius has a complaint, the courts are open. Arminian commentators see lawful process.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed commentators see civil order as God’s gift.

verses.text: But if you seek anything about other matters, it will be settled in the regular assembly.
verses.arminianNotes: Other matters should be settled in the lawful assembly. Arminian readers see order restored.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers see legitimate authority protecting the church.

verses.text: For indeed we are in danger of being accused concerning today’s riot, there being no cause. Concerning it, we wouldn’t be able to give an account of this commotion.”
verses.arminianNotes: They risk being charged with rioting. Arminian expositors see self-interest calming the crowd.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed expositors see God using ordinary concerns to protect his people.

verses.text: When he had thus spoken, he dismissed the assembly.
verses.arminianNotes: He dismisses the assembly. Arminian readers see the danger passing.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers see God’s servants preserved for further work.
